passage: Every time a client call went badly, Alka found herself on her phone for twenty minutes, thumb flicking, barely seeing anything. She had tried deleting the apps; she reinstalled them within the week. This time, at her office in Andheri, she tried something else. The cue would stay, that tight feeling after a hard call, but the answer would change. When a call ended, she would take the stairwell, down two floors and back up, breathing slowly. In a small notebook she ticked each time: walk or scroll, and how she felt afterwards. Jasleen, at the next desk, noticed the ticks. "What's that?" "Stairs versus scrolling," Alka said. By the end of the month the walk column was longer, and beside it she had written: "calmer, and I don't lose the afternoon."

qa.q: What did Alka tick in her small notebook?
qa.a: Walk or scroll, and how she felt afterwards.

qa.q: Why did deleting the apps not work for Alka?
qa.a: The stress after a hard call still needed an outlet, so without something else to meet that need she went back and reinstalled them.

qa.q: What choice made the change stick this time?
qa.a: Keeping the same cue but swapping the response for a stairwell walk with slow breathing, and tracking the result so she could see it worked.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the "stairs versus scrolling" notebook?
qa.a: Jasleen may find it odd at first but interesting, seeing a colleague handle hard calls without disappearing into her phone.

grounding: An adult keeps the stress cue but replaces scrolling with a stairwell walk and tracks how it feels.

"Varun bhaiya, you've been on that phone since you walked in."
"Bad day. It helps."
Nitin sat on the arm of the sofa. "Does it?"
"For a bit." Varun kept scrolling. "Then I feel worse and keep going."
"You tried quitting last month."

Varun laughed. "That's so Papa."
"Try it for a week. Write down how you feel after each one, phone or balcony."
A week later a sheet hung on the fridge: five balcony ticks, two phone ticks, and "balcony = actually calmer" in Varun's messy handwriting.

passage: Last spring my scrolling got bad. Every evening after my shift at the pharmacy I'd sit on the bed, tell myself "five minutes", and surface an hour later with stinging eyes, more wound up than before. I kept trying to just stop. It never lasted, because the need didn't go away: I was stressed and wanted a break. My friend Imran said, "Don't take the break away. Change what the break is." So I kept the same moment, sitting on the bed after work, and swapped the phone for five minutes of slow breathing by the open window. I made a chart and marked every evening: breathing or phone, and a number for how I felt. It took three weeks and some bad nights. But the breathing column won. I'm Usha, and I still sit on that bed every evening.

qa.q: What did Usha swap the phone for?
qa.a: Five minutes of slow breathing by the open window.

qa.q: Why did just stopping never last for Usha?
qa.a: The need behind the scrolling, stress and wanting a break, was still there, so without another way to meet it the phone kept winning.

qa.q: What choice made the change work, and what helped it last?
qa.a: Keeping the same moment on the bed but changing what the break was, and marking a chart each evening so the calmer nights became visible.

qa.q: How might Imran feel hearing that the breathing column won?
qa.a: Imran may feel glad the advice helped, and pleased that Usha stuck with it through three weeks and some bad nights.

grounding: An adult keeps the after-work cue but replaces stress scrolling with breathing, tracking results until it holds.

Staff wellbeing session notes, 18 June. Ishita, counsellor.
Aditi, a call-centre team lead, came in about what she called "stress scrolling". After a hard customer call she reaches for her phone and scrolls for fifteen or twenty minutes. She has deleted the apps twice and reinstalled them within days. We talked about what the scrolling gives her: a break, a few minutes where nobody needs anything from her. So we kept the cue, the end of a hard call, and swapped the action: stand up, walk to the stairwell window and back, or three slow breaths if she can't leave the desk. She tracks it on a card, tick or cross. Today she showed me two weeks of cards, mostly ticks. "I still want the phone sometimes," she said. "But I don't need it the same way."

qa.q: How many times had Aditi deleted the apps?
qa.a: She has deleted the apps twice.

qa.q: Why does the scrolling feel so needed to Aditi after a hard call?
qa.a: Aditi feels stressed and drained after a hard call, and scrolling gives her a short break where nobody needs anything from her; without something else meeting that need, she keeps pulling the apps back.

qa.q: What choice did Ishita and Aditi make, and why did it work better than deleting?
qa.a: They kept the same cue, the end of a hard call, and swapped the action for a stairwell walk or three breaths, so Aditi still gets her break, and the card shows how it goes.

qa.q: How might Aditi's team experience the change?
qa.a: The team may find her back sooner and more present after tough calls, since a short walk gives her the pause without pulling her into a screen.

passage: The phone calls from parents always came at the end of the school day in Sirsi, and they always left Devika tense. passage: Fatima worked the customer complaints line at a furniture company in Warsaw. After a hard call, her hand went to her phone, and she'd scroll until her supervisor coughed. She had tried locking the phone in her drawer. Then she just sat staring at the drawer, tense and irritable. Marek, who sat opposite, mentioned that he stood at the window after bad calls. So Fatima tried it: call ends, headset off, walk to the window, three slow breaths, look at the trams. Back. On a sticky note, she kept a tally: window or phone. On the first Friday, it was four windows and seven phones. By the third Friday, eleven windows and two phones. "Still need a break," she told Marek. "Just a different one." He nodded. The trams below kept moving, and Fatima's shoulders felt a little looser.

qa.a: Eleven windows and two phones.

qa.q: Why did locking the phone away leave Fatima tense and irritable?
qa.a: The hard calls still left her needing relief, and with nothing to replace scrolling, she felt stuck and frustrated staring at the drawer.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Fatima, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same cue but swapping in the window and breathing worked, because it still gave her the break she needed, and the tally showed her progress.

qa.q: How does Marek influence Fatima's change?
qa.a: Marek shares his own window habit casually, giving Fatima an idea without pushing her, and later quietly supports her with a nod.

grounding: It shows an adult who keeps the stressful cue but replaces scrolling with breathing at a window and tracks the result, meeting the same need for a break.

passage:
The nurses' station at the city hospital was busy even at 3 p.m. Sunaina, twenty-five, had a pattern: every time a difficult relative left the desk, she grabbed her phone and scrolled. Five minutes, sometimes fifteen. Afterward she felt more drained, not less.
Her colleague Pradeep suggested, “Don't just stop. Replace it. When you feel that rush, walk to the end of the corridor and back. Or do the four-count breathing at the window.”
So she tried. Same trigger: a tense conversation. New action: a walk to the corridor window, four slow breaths. On a scrap of paper in her pocket she tallied how she felt after, on a scale from one to five.
After two weeks, the tally was mostly fours. The scrolling sheet from the week before had been mostly twos.
The stress still came. But the walk met the need.

qa.q: What did Sunaina tally on the scrap of paper?
qa.a: How she felt after each walk, on a scale from one to five.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina reach for the phone after difficult conversations?
qa.a: She felt stressed and wanted quick relief, even though scrolling left her more drained.

qa.q: Why did replacing the scrolling work better than simply stopping?
qa.a: The same cue now led to a walk and breathing that met her need for relief, and tracking showed it helped.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel seeing Sunaina's tally of mostly fours?
qa.a: Pradeep would probably feel glad and a little proud that the suggestion helped.

grounding: The passage shows an adult keeping the stress cue but swapping scrolling for a short walk and breathing, and tracking the result.

passage:
Dear Jasleen,

You asked how I stopped doom-scrolling at work. I didn't stop, exactly. I swapped.

For months, every time my manager sent a tense message, I'd open my phone and scroll news for twenty minutes. I felt worse afterwards, but I kept doing it. It was the only break I gave myself.

So I kept the trigger and changed the action. Tense message arrives → I stand up, walk to the stairwell, go down one floor and back up. Then three slow breaths at the window.

I kept a small tally on a sticky note: how stressed before, how stressed after. The walk won almost every time.

It isn't magic. But I still get my break, just a better one.

Love,
Rashmi

qa.a: Rashmi walks to the stairwell, down one floor and back up.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel after scrolling news for twenty minutes?

qa.q: How might Jasleen react to Rashmi's method?

You asked how I got my screen time down, Manjula. I'll be honest: I didn't just delete the apps. I tried that. It lasted two days.
I'm Divyansh. I scroll when I'm stressed. Client yells, I scroll. Deadline moves, I scroll. It gives me a break, sort of. Then I feel worse.

And I tracked it. Just a line in my notes app: stress before, stress after, what I did. After three weeks it was obvious. Walks helped. Scrolling didn't.
The need didn't go away. I still need a break when I'm stressed. I just stopped giving myself the one that didn't work.

I sit across from Ramesh in the claims office, so I notice things. For most of last year, every time a difficult client email arrived, he'd sigh, pick up his phone and scroll for ten, fifteen minutes. Then go back to the email looking just as grim.
About two months ago that changed. Now when a hard email lands, he reads it, stands up and walks to the stairwell. I've timed it once: about five minutes. I can't tell what's going on inside him. But he looks less tired at five o'clock than he used to, and his phone stays face down.

"Vikas, you're scrolling again after that client call. Sit, I'll tell you about Chinmay-sir's own bad years.
When I was about your age, twenty-five, I had a manager who shouted on every call. After each one I'd grab my phone and scroll for twenty minutes. Nothing I saw ever helped. I'd go back to my desk still boiling.
Then I tried just stopping. No phone after calls. That lasted three days. My hands didn't know what to do, and the anger had nowhere to go.
So I changed tactics. After each bad call I still took a break, I didn't fight that. But instead of the phone I did slow breathing on the terrace, four counts in, six out, for three minutes. I marked a dot on my desk calendar each time.
In a month, the calendar was full of dots, and I wasn't boiling any more."

qa.a: He breathed four counts in and six out, for three minutes.

qa.q: How did young Chinmay feel when he tried simply stopping the phone?
qa.a: He felt restless and still angry, because his hands had nothing to do and the anger had nowhere to go.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chinmay's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: He kept the break after each call but swapped scrolling for breathing on the terrace and marked dots on a calendar, which still met his need to cool down.

"You look less fried," Jomon said on Friday.
